At Collider, David started as a Senior Writer in late 2022 and has been a Senior Editor since mid-2023. He is in charge of ideating compelling and engaging List articles by working closely with writers, both Senior and Junior, as well as other editors. Occasionally, David also reviews movies and TV shows and writes episode recaps. Currently, David is also writing his second novel, a psychological horror satire that will, hopefully, be picked up for publication sometime next year.

Science fiction is one of the best genres for complex, introspective examinations of human nature. Although ostensibly concerned with the future of humanity and all the technological possibilities that can come with it, sci-fi is, at its core, about our ever-changing relationship with the world around us. The genre thrives on studies about the human psyche clashing against accelerated change, and how we as a species evolve as a consequence.

No book better explores these thematic concerns than David Mitchell's 2004 masterpiece Cloud Atlas. The ambitious and sprawling novel tells a series of stories across millennia, balancing both historical fiction and metafiction to produce one of the most original and wholly distinct works of the new millennium. Among its many strengths, Cloud Atlas also has what could be the best final line in modern sci-fi, a deceptively simple but no less powerful sentiment that perfectly encapsulates the book's themes and sci-fi's larger concern with human nature.
What Is 'Cloud Atlas' About?

Cloud Atlas has a singular structure, composed of six distinct stories, each one experienced somehow by the protagonist of the next one. The first five stories appear chronologically and end in a cliffhanger, leading to a self-contained sixth story set in a post-apocalyptic future. From there, each of the original stories picks up where it left off in reverse chronological order.

The five stories are: "The Pacific Journal of Adam Ewing," about an American lawyer suffering from a mysterious poisoning during his voyage throughout the Pacific; "Letters from Zedelghem," about Robert Frobisher, a struggling composer entering a complex arrangement with aging composer Vyvyan Ayrs; "Half-Lives: The First Luisa Rey Mystery," about journalist Luisa Rey's investigation into corruption and targeted assassination at the HYDRA nuclear plant; "The Gasthly Ordeal of Timothy Cavendish," about an elderly book publisher who is tricked into committing himself to a brutal nursing home; and "An Orison of Sonmi-451," about a clone who joins a rebellion against the state's corporate culture. The central sixth story, "Sloosha's Crossin' an' Evrythin' After," is set in a post-apocalyptic Earth and follows a tribal man and a woman from an advanced society as they make their way to the ruins of the Mauna Kea Observatories to learn a hidden truth.

Cloud Atlas has often received rave reviews, with praise going to its bold and grand narrative, structure, character work, worldbuilding, and thematic concerns. Criticisms often highlight how the book's reach far exceeds its grasp and how it can feel incomplete in its ambitions. A film adaptation came out in 2012, co-written and co-directed by the Wachowskis and Tom Tykwer and starring an ensemble cast including Oscar winners Tom Hanks, Halle Berry, and Jim Broadbent alongside Ben Whishaw, Hugh Grant, Hugo Weaving, Jim Sturgess, and Doona Bae. The film is a solid translation of a novel once thought to be unfilmmable, even if some of its creative choices are a bit hard to accept.
What Is 'Cloud Atlas' Final Line?
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F68b2869467189-David%20Caballero%202.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/cloud-atlas-book0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Random House

Because of the book's reverse chronological approach, the narrative ends with the second part of "The Pacific Journal of Adam Ewing." Set in the mid-18th century, the story mainly centers on the titular character's awakening to the injustices around him, first by witnessing the brutalization of a Moriori man named Autua, whom he helps secure work aboard the ship en route to Hawaii. Once Ewing discovers that he is being poisoned by his presumed friend, Dr. Henry Goose, he is too weak to stop it or defend himself before being saved by Autua. Realizing he owes his life to Autua, Ewing decides to join the abolitionist movement.

Reuniting with his wife and her family, Ewing declares his ambitions. His pro-slavery father-in-law dismisses the idea of abolition, claiming that whatever efforts he can actually muster will ultimately amount to nothing, just "a single drop in a limitless ocean." Proud and certain of his choice, and fully supported by his loving wife, Ewing fires back at the man, delivering one of the most beautifully constructed lines in modern sci-fi: "What is an ocean but a multitude of drops?" Thus, Cloud Atlas ends its larger-than-life, millennia-spanning narrative with a simple but potent and evergreen sentiment that perfectly sums up not only the book's lofty ambitions but also captures one of the true purposes of sci-fi as a genre: to show the impact of one life across time and space.
Why Is 'Cloud Atlas' Final Line Still Powerful?
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/cloud-atlas-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Sceptre

At first glance, this quote might seem simple and not particularly groundbreaking. After all, the power of one individual in the grand scope of things is an idea that has been constantly explored in numerous works across multiple genres. Yet, there's something beautiful in the way Mitchell presents his final statement. For starters, the quote has an undeniable lyricism to it; it's just a romantic way of presenting a straightforward idea, adding not only literary flair but also a layer of poetry to it.

Secondly, there's the importance the quote plays in Adam Ewing's story. Ewing is not a bad man, but he begins his story woefully unaware of the injustices that surround him. Through him, Mitchell explores how easy it is to blind oneself to the realities of the world when cruelty is normalized in society. Ewinng has to literally come near the brink of death to understand that his life must have a higher purpose, that he can indeed make a difference, not only in Autua's life but in the lives of so many others.

Finally, there's the meaning that the quote has in the context of science fiction. Some of the greatest works in literature, from The Lord of the Rings to Brave New World, follow rousing stories about individuals sparking a change through their choices. In Cloud Atlas, Ewing's words and actions reverberate across time and space. His mid-18th-century diaries find Robert Frobisher in 1931, whose letters help Luisa Rey in 1975. Luisa's expose book awakens Cavendish's rebellious spirit against the nursing home's staff in the 2000s, and his autobiography later inspires Sonmi's spiritual awakening in the 22nd century. Sonmi later becomes a deity in the post-apocalyptic world, with her final testimony becoming doctrine.

Here, we see how one singular man put in motion a chain of events that spanned millennia and inspired countless deeds, as small as a love letter and as big as a complete uprising against a corporate state. One drop could indeed be strong enough to move an entire ocean, starting with a ripple that eventually became a wave before disappearing beyond the horizon. Cloud Atlas is truly one of the best sci-fi books of the 2000s, and its powerful final declaration is just one of the main reasons why.
